title: Start With the Willing
author: Angela Langlands
summary: Langlands answers the question of how to build a prototype team for a new school model, such as an interdependent learning community. Her answer is that you cannot build the first team from a mix of willing and unwilling educators, because early on there is no momentum to absorb the drag. She offers a boat metaphor of speedboat, dinghy, cruise ship, dock and anchor, and insists these are boats and not people, since teachers move between them as confidence, support and circumstances change. She separates willingness from fit, noting that an eager teacher may not suit a given age group and an experienced one may refuse an interdependent model. Her tactics for moving people on the dock include open doors for observation, a clear direction, watching students and parent ambassadors. The practical advice for administrators is to give dinghies a tow rope, protect the speedboat crew, interview for willingness as well as experience, and remember that leadership itself must be willing.
points: Start a new initiative with a willing prototype team, because momentum later does the work that persuasion cannot do at the start.
Treat resistance positions as temporary boats, not fixed identities, and recognise that overwhelm and a change of heart can look the same from outside.
Willingness and fit are different: choose people who will learn and share responsibility, and do not assume the most experienced teacher is the right pick.
Open classrooms to observation to move sceptics, since seeing the work is more persuasive than any presentation or PD session.
Protect the early adopters from exhaustion and give inexperienced but willing staff practical support, not encouragement alone.
quotes: You can’t build a prototype team with a combination of willing and unwilling educators. Either people are ready to jump on the speedboat, or they’re in a dinghy, paddling hard to catch up.
But here’s an important distinction. These are boats, not people. People move between them.

You can have a willing educator who isn’t necessarily the best fit for a particular prototype. You can also have someone with tremendous experience who isn’t willing to work in an interdependent model.
Open doors. Inviting people in to observe moved entire teams at once. Sometimes seeing the work in action is more convincing than any presentation, explanation, or professional development session.

Direction. For some, it was simply knowing the school was heading this way and deciding they’d rather work here than not. That moves people, but it’s a thinner reason to board the boat. Compliance isn’t the same as commitment.

And when that many people are moving in the same direction towards shore, the anchors don’t have much leverage anymore. That’s the other half of what those leaders told me. A prototype needs a willing crew, because there’s no momentum yet to absorb the drag.
People who are willing but inexperienced need practical support, not simply encouragement to try harder.
